# A Brief Discussion of the Birthday "Paradox"

The problem we discussed last time was:

> In a room with $n$ people, what is the minimum number of people required so that at least two of them have birthday on the same day with probability at least $50\%$.

## Probabilistic Approach

We saw last time, that the formula for this is:

$$p=1-\prod_{i=0}^{n-1}\frac{365-i}{365}.$$

We can now verify for which value of $n$ we obtain for the first time $p>0.5$:

```{r}
# In R we prefer to assign using `<-` instead of `=`.
p <- 0
for (n in 2:365) { # We start with 2, since 1 person cannot have the same b-day with somebody else.
  product <- 1 # We initialise products to 1 in order to avoid getting such at 0
  for (i in 0:(n-1)) {
    product <- product * (365 - i) / 365
  }
  p <- 1 - product
  if (p > 0.5) {
    # Stop once we encounter a p greater than 50%.
    print(paste("The minimum value of n is:", n))
    break
  }
}
```

## Statistical Approach

Instead of making theoretical calculations with probabilities, we can try and run a statistical simulation, as follows:

```{r}
N <- 1000 # Number of trials
for (n in 2:365) {
  # We first create a sample of n randomly chosen bdays
  # `sample()` picks a uniformly random sample from a certain list of values.
  hits <- 0
  for (i in 1:N) {
    bdays <- sample(1:365, n, replace = TRUE)
    # Keep only different dates.
    unique_bdays <- unique(bdays)
    if (length(bdays) > length(unique_bdays)) {
      # In this case, (at least) two people share b-day.
      hits <- hits + 1
    }
  }
  p <- hits / N
  if (p > 0.5) {
    print(paste("The minimum value of n is:", n))
    break
  }
}
```

What we see here, by running the above chunk a few times, is that we get the correct answer (maybe 24, as well) with a good chance.
